```{r}
# Part Two Question 1
library(tidyverse) # loads packages
library(rvest)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
communityareas<-read_html("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_areas_of_Chicago") # loads the html file


#EXTRACT TABLE AS DATAFRAME
CAtable <- communityareas %>%
  html_element("table") %>%
  html_table()

head(CAtable)

FinalCAtable<- CAtable[-c(1,79),] %>% # removes rows 1 & 79 from original
  select(No.,Name,Population) %>% # only keeps the number name and population
  mutate(
    Population = str_remove_all(Population,","),
    Population = as.numeric(Population) # removes comma and makes population numeric
)

FinalCAtable %>% slice(24) # West Town

FinalCAtable %>%  # Arranges population high to low then gets top 5
  arrange(desc(Population)) %>%
  head(5)

```

```{r, part 1 question2}
library(readr)
bookhtml <- read_html("https://books.toscrape.com/")


eachbook <- bookhtml |> # each book section
  html_elements("article.product_pod")
eachbook

title = eachbook |> #title of each book
  html_element("h3") |> 
  html_text2()
title


price = eachbook |> #price of each book
  html_element("p.price_color") |> 
  html_text2()
price


availability = eachbook |>  #availility of each book
  html_element("p.instock.availability") |> 
  html_text2()
availability

bookstoscrape <- tibble( # creates table
  title, 
  price,
  availability
)



cleanbookstoscrape <-bookstoscrape %>% # cleans table and makes price numeric
   mutate(
    price = str_remove_all(price,"£"),
    price = as.numeric(price)
)

write_csv(cleanbookstoscrape, "books.csv") # saves table as csv and in repo

```

```{r part 3}
library(httr)
library(jsonlite)

# answer to part 3 question 1
url <- "https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/v6vf-nfxy.json"

params <- list( #creates a filter that will go through API
  community_area = "24",
   `$where` = "created_date >= '2026-01-01T00:00:00'",
  `$order` = "created_date DESC",
  `$limit` = 1000
)
res <- GET(url, query = params)

#question 2
dat <- fromJSON(content(res, "text")) # dataframe created fromJSON 
head(dat)

nrow(dat) #number of rows

colnames(dat) #column names


dat %>% 
  count(sr_type, sort = TRUE)%>% # uses data frame and sorts by sr type from descending order then gives top 10. Answer to 3
  head(10)
```

• Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income, “Total”: B25070_001E • Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income, "50.0 percent or more":B25070_010E • Median Household Income: B19013_001E

```{r}

# step 2 creates dataset for Ohio with all 3 variables for all Ohio counties
Ohioincome <- get_acs(geography = "tract", 
                   variables = c(
                     percent_rent_total = "B25070_001", # gets all 3 variables
                     fiftypercent_rent="B25070_010",
                       median_householdinc= "B19013_001" ),
                   state = "OH", , 
                   year = 2024, 
                   survey = "acs5") 
head(Ohioincome) 
```
```{r}
library(tidyr)
library(janitor)

# step 3
wideOhioIncome <-Ohioincome  %>% #uses Ohioincome dataset and gets rid of moe
  select(-moe)%>%
separate_wider_delim( #used AI here to figure out how to seperate the name into different columns
    cols = NAME,
    delim = "; ",
    names = c("census_tract", "county", "state")
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider( #makes it wider by giving each variable its own column
    id_cols = c(GEOID,census_tract,county,state),
    names_from = variable,
    values_from = c(estimate),
  ) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
#step 3.2
  mutate( # adds  variable to table
    severe_burden_rate = fiftypercent_rent/ percent_rent_total
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(severe_burden_rate))
print(wideOhioIncome)

```
STEP Four
```{r}
#gets median and mode for severe burden rate
wideOhioIncome %>%
  summarise(
    mean_inc   = mean(severe_burden_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_inc = median(severe_burden_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

#2
countyrates <- wideOhioIncome %>% #groups by county gets mean and arranges them
  group_by(county) %>%
  summarise(avg_rate = mean(severe_burden_rate, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_rate))

#top 5 highest rates
head(countyrates, 5)

#top 5 lowest rates
tail(countyrates, 5)
```
Step 5

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

#creates scatterplot
ggplot(data = wideOhioIncome, aes(x = median_householdinc, y = severe_burden_rate)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", se = FALSE) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Median Household Income vs. Severe Burden Rate",
    subtitle = "Ohio Census Tracts",
    x = "Median Household Income ($)",
    y = "Severe Burden Rate"
  ) +

  theme_minimal()


#creates bar graph

top_5 <- head(countyrates, 5)
low_5 <- tail(countyrates, 5)

#getting them to be percentages 
countybargraph <- bind_rows(top_5, low_5) %>%
  mutate(avg_ratepercent = avg_rate * 100)


ggplot(countybargraph, aes(x = avg_ratepercent, y = reorder(county, avg_ratepercent))) + # orders from high to low
  geom_col( fill = "blue") +
  labs(
    title = "Top 5 and Bottom 5 Counties by Severe Housing Burden Rate",
    subtitle = "Ohio Counties",
    x = "Average Severe Housing Burden Rate (%)",
    y = "County"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Step 6:
1. What relationship do you see between income and severe rent burden in Ohio, and what might
explain it? 

The relationship I see is that as median household income increases the severe burden rate decreases which makes sense. If the income increases, they are more likely to afford their rent compared to others who have lower income who make enough to cover rent but are limited with other things.

2. What are two limitations of using county-level ACS estimates to decide where to target rental
assistance? 

One limitation is that at county-level there could be drastic ranges of income in a single county. A really wealthy neighborhood vs an impoverished neighborhood which can skew the numbers. Another limitation is that it is every 5 years and a lot can happen in that time span that can change the circumstances at each county.

Part 5:

1.  The 311 dataset includes the street address and coordinates of each request.
Suppose you wanted to publish a map of West Town requests on your GitHub Page. Identify one
privacy risk, then explain how you would apply one de-identification technique before
publishing.

Answer: One privacy risk is that when making a map, it will show what area exactly in West Town is having certain issues. If there is a rodent problem, it exposes people who live nearby when most likely they would want to not have that type of issue made public and just have it resolved. One technique I would apply is aggregation. I would use summary statistics and get total counts for issues instead of just doing each individual requests. I would also just get of exact street address as well. 


2. Bias and data quality. 311 data shows where people report problems, which is not
always where problems exist. Explain how this could mislead a city manager who assigns repair
crews by request counts, and describe one way to check for or reduce that bias.

Answer:This could mislead a city manager because they would send crews to the area where people only report the problems and not other areas where problems also exist. This would mean the crews would be sent only where requested and leaves other areas who may not report to be unserved or served to a lesser degree which is not appropriate.  One way to reduce this bias is to be proactive and find which areas report less. It may not be because there is no issues but less reporting. Going into these areas and informing residents about how to report but also checking if there are issues.


3. Scraping responsibly.  Using the criteria discussed in Week 5, explain whether the
scraping you did in Part II was appropriate. Then describe one civic data situation where you
should not scrape without further review.

Answer: I would say the scraping I did in part 2 was appropriate. The data was on Wikipedia which was public, it was not about private individuals and it was also factual. A civic data situation where it would not be appropriate is when it is not public and can also about an individual. It can be a government website that collects an individuals data such as name, address and phone number. Scraping that is non-consensual and most likely is not data that is available for the public.
